title: Sultanate of Malacca
capsule: The Sultanate of Malacca was a Malay Muslim sultanate founded around 1400 by Paramesvara, a Srivijayan prince who established a trading port at the tip of the Malay Peninsula that rapidly became the principal entrepôt of Southeast Asian maritime commerce. At its apex under Sultan Muzaffar Shah and his successor Mansur Shah (mid-15th century), Malacca controlled the Strait of Malacca, extracted tribute from ports across Sumatra and the Malay world, and served as the primary hub through which spices, Chinese porcelain, and Indian textiles circulated between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea. The sultanate fell to a Portuguese fleet under Afonso de Albuquerque in 1511; the royal court fled to Johor and Perak, establishing successor states that kept the Malacca political tradition alive long after the Portuguese occupation.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The Malacca Sultanate's core territory on the Malay Peninsula is attested through Portuguese accounts (Tome Pires' Suma Oriental), Chinese Ming diplomatic records, and Malay chronicles (Sejarah Melayu); the outer extent of tributary relationships with Sumatran and Malay ports is broadly inferred from these narrative sources rather than mapped administrative records.
